operations.evidence: police recorded crime covers a wider range of offences than the CSEW; it covers populations outside the household survey scope; it includes lower-volume offences such as homicide.
broader coverage does not imply complete coverage; source populations and offence definitions differ from CSEW.
police recorded crime misses offences not reported to police; it also misses offences not recorded by police; trends can change with recording practices police activity and public reporting.
long-term trend comparisons require recording-context metadata; recorded volume is not direct victimisation prevalence.

Home Office Counting Rules changed in May 2023 for conduct crimes; the requirement to record two crimes in specified same-victim same-perpetrator reports was removed; the change created statistical discontinuity in affected offence groups.
police still investigate reported offences; pre- and post-change volumes are not directly interchangeable.

the May 2023 rule change reduced some offences associated with conduct crimes; malicious communications was cited as an affected category; stalking and harassment recording increased in the changed classification context.
the size of the impact is difficult to measure; changes in offence mix must not be read as direct changes in total harm.
the March 2026 bulletin uses a police-recorded snapshot taken on 8 June 2026; the snapshot covers data up to March 2026; later revisions may differ from the snapshot.
snapshot date is not the date every crime occurred; snapshot figures are revision-sensitive.
police recorded around 5.2 million crimes excluding fraud and computer misuse; the reported annual movement was a 1 percent decrease; the comparison level for the previous year was about 5.3 million.
the national count excludes fraud and computer misuse; the count is not a parcel or LSOA rate.

the CSEW estimated 40.9 percent experienced or witnessed anti-social behaviour; the increase was partly inflated by question changes from April 2025; ONS scheduled supporting methodology for 25 August 2026.
the estimate combines experienced or witnessed ASB; pre-change and post-change values require question-version context.

police recorded about one million anti-social behaviour incidents including BTP; the level was described as similar to the previous year; HMICFRS inspections found recording improvements were needed in many forces.
police ASB incidents and CSEW ASB experience are different measures; recording quality varies between forces.
NDQIS flags offences involving knives; it also flags domestic abuse child sexual abuse and online crime; flagging operates across four police collections.
automated flags require source-record quality; a flag is not a confirmed offence characteristic without validation.
NDQIS is available to 42 forces; usage information is reported in relevant datasets; availability does not mean identical use by every force.
the unavailable force and usage differences must remain explicit; tool availability is not proof of complete flag coverage.
police recorded 6.7 million crimes in year ending September 2025; the level was similar to the previous year; the bulletin compared this with 4.2 million in year ending March 2015.
the series includes offence groups with recording discontinuities; the national total is not a local rate.

ONS said increases since March 2015 were largely driven by police activity and recording practices; some movement may reflect genuine crime changes; police recorded crime is not generally a reliable indicator of overall crime trends.
the statement concerns overall trends rather than every offence type; recording influence does not mean all growth is artificial.

police recorded crime provides insight into lower-volume higher-harm offences; examples include homicide and weapons offences; robbery is another offence type highlighted for police-recorded analysis.
fitness remains dependent on reporting and recording quality; higher harm is not a numeric parcel score.
CSEW estimates are accredited official statistics; police recorded crime data are not accredited official statistics; the two designations must be retained separately.
accreditation does not remove survey uncertainty; non-accreditation does not make all police data unusable.
ONS corrected two figure data-point dates on 10 April 2026; the corrected labels were year ending September 2024 and September 2025; ONS stated that no data values changed.
metadata corrections and data corrections must be distinguished; superseded versions should not be silently mixed.
CSEW estimates for year ending March 2021 are unavailable; estimates for year ending March 2022 are also unavailable; the gap resulted from suspension of face-to-face interviewing.
missing survey years are not zero crime; telephone-survey outputs require separate mode metadata.
Report Fraud launched on 4 December 2025; the system replaced Action Fraud for national fraud and cybercrime reporting; ONS said subsequent bulletins would no longer refer to Action Fraud.
system transition can create series and processing changes; launch date is not an incident-date boundary.
the December 2025 crime release was published on 23 April 2026; CSEW content was labelled accredited official statistics; police recorded crime content was labelled official statistics.
designation is component-specific within the release; release date differs from the reference period.
the release provides personal and household crime open tables; tables include demographic and household breakdowns; incidence and prevalence are published as separate products.
open-table combinations can have different bases and precision; national survey tables do not supply parcel observations.
